topics: Adjugate formula, Cramer's rule & volume scaling

body.en: The determinant is the unique multilinear, alternating scalar functional on square matrices that measures the volume scaling factor and orientation change induced by a linear transformation. Its non-zero status completely characterizes matrix invertibility, while its algebraic properties provide the foundational connection between algebra and geometry.

blocks.heading: Level 1 · Foundations — Axiomatic Definition, Laplace Cofactor Expansion & Triangular Matrices

body.en: The determinant can be defined axiomatically through three characterizing properties, or constructively via recursive cofactor expansion along any row or column.

label.en: ● Definition 4.1 — Axiomatic Characterization & Laplace Cofactor Expansion

body.en:
1. The Three Axioms of the Determinant: The determinant \( \det: \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \to \mathbb{R} \) is the unique function satisfying:
• Multilinearity in Rows: \( \det \) is linear with respect to each individual row when all other rows are held fixed.
• Alternating Property: Swapping any two rows negates the determinant: \( \det(R_1, \dots, R_j, \dots, R_i, \dots, R_n) = -\det(R_1, \dots, R_i, \dots, R_j, \dots, R_n) \). If two rows are identical, \( \det(A) = 0 \).
• Normalization: \( \det(I_n) = 1 \).

2. Laplace Cofactor Expansion: For any chosen row \( i \) (or column \( j \)): \[ \det(A) = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} C_{ij} = \sum_{j=1}^n (-1)^{i+j} a_{ij} \det(M_{ij}), \] where \( M_{ij} \) is the \( (n-1) \times (n-1) \) minor submatrix formed by deleting row \( i \) and column \( j \), and \( C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} \det(M_{ij}) \) is the cofactor.

3. Triangular Matrices: If \( A \) is upper-triangular, lower-triangular, or diagonal, its determinant is simply the product of its main diagonal entries: \[ \det(A) = a_{11} a_{22} \dots a_{nn} = \prod_{i=1}^n a_{ii}. \]

label.en: Level 1 (Foundations) — Worked Example · Cofactor Expansion Strategy

body.en:
Problem: Evaluate \( \det(A) \) for the \( 3 \times 3 \) matrix by expanding along the row or column with the most zeros: \[ A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 5 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}. \]

Step 1 · Choose Optimal Expansion Path:
Row 2 contains two zeros (\( a_{21} = 0, a_{23} = 0 \)), leaving only \( a_{22} = 4 \).

Step 2 · Apply Laplace Expansion along Row 2: \[ \det(A) = (-1)^{2+1}(0)\det(M_{21}) + (-1)^{2+2}(4)\det(M_{22}) + (-1)^{2+3}(0)\det(M_{23}). \] \[ \det(A) = 4 \det(M_{22}) = 4 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 6 \end{vmatrix}. \]

Step 3 · Evaluate 2×2 Minor: \[ \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 6 \end{vmatrix} = (2)(6) - (-3)(1) = 12 + 3 = 15. \] \[ \det(A) = 4(15) = \mathbf{60}. \]

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

Evaluate the determinant of the \( 4 \times 4 \) triangular matrix: \[ T = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -2 & 7 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 5 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 5 \end{pmatrix}. \]

solution.en: Since \( T \) is upper-triangular, its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries: \[ \det(T) = (3)(-1)(2)(5) = \mathbf{-30}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Geometric Volume Interpretation & The Multiplicative Property

body.en: Geometrically, \( |\det(A)| \) represents the hypervolume of the \( n \)-dimensional parallelotope spanned by the column vectors of \( A \). Under a linear mapping \( T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} \), any region \( S \subset \mathbb{R}^n \) with volume \( V(S) \) is mapped to an image with volume \( |\det(A)| V(S) \).

figure.title: Determinant as Signed Area of Parallelogram

caption.en: Parallelogram in \( \mathbb{R}^2 \) spanned by vectors \( \mathbf{u} = \langle 3, 0 \rangle \) and \( \mathbf{v} = \langle 1, 2 \rangle \). The determinant \( \det\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = (3)(2) - (1)(0) = 6 \) represents the exact geometric area of the parallelogram.

label.en: ● Theorem 4.1 & Proof · The Multiplicative Property det(AB) = det(A)det(B)

body.en:
Theorem: For any \( n \times n \) matrices \( A \) and \( B \): \[ \det(AB) = \det(A) \det(B). \]

Proof via Elementary Matrices:
1. If \( E \) is an elementary matrix:
• Row interchange: \( \det(E) = -1 \), and \( \det(EA) = -\det(A) = \det(E)\det(A) \).
• Row scaling by \( c \): \( \det(E) = c \), and \( \det(EA) = c\det(A) = \det(E)\det(A) \).
• Row replacement: \( \det(E) = 1 \), and \( \det(EA) = \det(A) = \det(E)\det(A) \).
Hence for any elementary matrix \( E \), \( \det(EB) = \det(E)\det(B) \).
2. By induction, if \( A = E_1 E_2 \dots E_k \) is invertible: \[ \det(AB) = \det(E_1 \dots E_k B) = \det(E_1)\dots\det(E_k)\det(B) = \det(E_1 \dots E_k)\det(B) = \det(A)\det(B). \]
3. If \( A \) is not invertible, then \( \text{rank}(A) < n \implies \text{rank}(AB) \le \text{rank}(A) < n \), so \( AB \) is also not invertible. Thus \( \det(AB) = 0 \) and \( \det(A)\det(B) = 0 \cdot \det(B) = 0 \).
Therefore \( \det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B) \) holds universally. \(\blacksquare\)

Corollaries:
• Transpose: \( \det(A^T) = \det(A) \).
• Inverse: If \( A \) is invertible, \( \det(A^{-1}) = \frac{1}{\det(A)} \).
• Scalar Multiple: \( \det(c A) = c^n \det(A) \) for \( n \times n \) matrix \( A \).

label.en: Level 2 (Medium) — Worked Example · Fast Determinant via Row Reduction

body.en:
Problem: Evaluate the determinant of \( A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \) using Gaussian row operations.

Step 1 · Row Replacement on Column 1:
Perform \( R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1 \) and \( R_4 \leftarrow R_4 - R_1 \) (row replacements leave determinant unchanged): \[ \det(A) = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}. \]

Step 2 · Row Swap to place pivot in Row 2:
Perform \( R_2 \leftrightarrow R_3 \) (multiplies determinant by \( -1 \)): \[ \det(A) = -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 1 \end{vmatrix}. \]

Step 3 · Eliminate Column 3 in Row 4:
Perform \( R_4 \leftarrow R_4 - R_3 \) (no change to determinant): \[ \det(A) = -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \end{vmatrix}. \]

Step 4 · Multiply Triangular Diagonal: \[ \det(A) = -(1)(3)(3)(2) = \mathbf{-18}. \]

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

Let \( A \) and \( B \) be \( 3 \times 3 \) matrices with \( \det(A) = 3 \) and \( \det(B) = -2 \). Compute the exact numerical value of: \[ \det\left( 2 A^2 B^{-1} A^T \right). \]

solution.en: Apply determinant algebraic properties for \( 3 \times 3 \) matrices: \[ \det(2 M) = 2^3 \det(M) = 8 \det(M). \] Using the multiplicative, power, transpose, and inverse properties: \[ \det(A^2 B^{-1} A^T) = [\det(A)]^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\det(B)} \cdot \det(A) = \frac{[\det(A)]^3}{\det(B)}. \] Substitute \( \det(A) = 3 \) and \( \det(B) = -2 \): \[ \det\left( 2 A^2 B^{-1} A^T \right) = 8 \cdot \frac{3^3}{-2} = 8 \cdot \frac{27}{-2} = 8(-13.5) = \mathbf{-108}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced / University Rigor — The Classical Adjugate, Cramer's Rule & Invertibility Invariant

body.en: The adjugate matrix provides an explicit analytical formula for the inverse of an arbitrary \( n \times n \) matrix, leading to Cramer's Rule for solving non-singular linear systems without row operations.

label.en: ● Theorem 4.2 & Proof · The Fundamental Adjugate Identity & Cramer's Rule

body.en:
Definition: Let \( C \) be the cofactor matrix of \( A \) with entries \( C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}\det(M_{ij}) \). The adjugate matrix \( \operatorname{adj}(A) \) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix: \[ \operatorname{adj}(A) = C^T, \qquad (\operatorname{adj}(A))_{ij} = C_{ji}. \]

Theorem (Fundamental Adjugate Identity): For any square matrix \( A \in \mathbb{R}^{n imes n} \): \[ A \operatorname{adj}(A) = \operatorname{adj}(A) A = \det(A) I_n. \] Consequently, if \( \det(A) eq 0 \), then \( A \) is invertible and: \[ A^{-1} = rac{1}{\det(A)} \operatorname{adj}(A). \]

Proof: Consider the \( (i, k) \)-th entry of the product \( A \operatorname{adj}(A) \): \[ (A \operatorname{adj}(A))_{ik} = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} (\operatorname{adj}(A))_{jk} = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij} C_{kj}. \] • If \( i = k \), this is precisely the Laplace cofactor expansion of \( \det(A) \) along row \( i \), yielding \( \det(A) \).
• If \( i eq k \), this represents the cofactor expansion along row \( k \) of a matrix whose \( k \)-th row has been replaced by row \( i \). Such a matrix has two identical rows (row \( i \) and row \( k \)), so its determinant is zero! (This is known as expansion by alien cofactors).
Thus \( (A \operatorname{adj}(A))_{ik} = \det(A) \delta_{ik} \), where \( \delta_{ik} \) is the Kronecker delta. Therefore \( A \operatorname{adj}(A) = \det(A) I_n \). \( lacksquare\)

Theorem (Cramer's Rule): Let \( A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} \) with \( \det(A) eq 0 \). Then the unique solution coordinates are given by: \[ x_i = rac{\det(A_i(\mathbf{b}))}{\det(A)}, \qquad i = 1, \dots, n, \] where \( A_i(\mathbf{b}) \) is the matrix obtained by replacing column \( i \) of \( A \) with the vector \( \mathbf{b} \).

1. Additivity Myth: In general, \( \det(A + B) \neq \det(A) + \det(B) \). For instance, \( I_2 + (-I_2) = 0 \), yet \( \det(I_2) + \det(-I_2) = 1 + 1 = 2 \neq 0 \).
  2. Scalar Multiple Power Rule: For an \( n \times n \) matrix, \( \det(c A) = c^n \det(A) \), NOT \( c \det(A) \). For a \( 4 \times 4 \) matrix, \( \det(-A) = (-1)^4 \det(A) = \det(A) \).
  3. Adjugate Transpose Transposition: The adjugate is \( \operatorname{adj}(A) = C^T \). Forgetting to transpose the cofactor matrix produces incorrect inverse entries off the main diagonal.

label.en: Level 3 (Advanced) — Worked Example · Cramer's Rule & Invertibility Characterization

body.en:
Problem: Solve the linear system for \( x_2 \) using Cramer's Rule: \[ \begin{aligned} 2x_1 + x_2 + x_3 &= 4 \\ x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 &= 1 \\ 3x_1 + 2x_2 - x_3 &= 3 \end{aligned} \]

Step 1 · Compute Coefficient Determinant \( \det(A) \): \[ \det(A) = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = 2((-1)(-1) - (2)(2)) - 1((1)(-1) - (2)(3)) + 1((1)(2) - (-1)(3)). \] \[ = 2(1 - 4) - 1(-1 - 6) + 1(2 + 3) = 2(-3) - 1(-7) + 1(5) = -6 + 7 + 5 = \mathbf{6}. \] Since \( \det(A) = 6 \neq 0 \), Cramer's Rule applies.

Step 2 · Replace Column 2 with \( \mathbf{b} = (4, 1, 3)^T \): \[ \det(A_2(\mathbf{b})) = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 3 & -1 \end{vmatrix}. \] Expand along row 1: \[ = 2((1)(-1) - (2)(3)) - 4((1)(-1) - (2)(3)) + 1((1)(3) - (1)(3)) \] \[ = 2(-1 - 6) - 4(-1 - 6) + 1(0) = 2(-7) - 4(-7) = -14 + 28 = \mathbf{14}. \]

Step 3 · Compute \( x_2 \): \[ x_2 = \frac{\det(A_2(\mathbf{b}))}{\det(A)} = \frac{14}{6} = \mathbf{\frac{7}{3}}. \]

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced / University Rigor

Let \( A \) be an invertible \( n \times n \) matrix with \( n \ge 2 \). Prove analytically that: \[ \det(\operatorname{adj}(A)) = [\det(A)]^{n-1}. \]

solution.en:
Step 1 · Use the Fundamental Adjugate Identity: \[ A \operatorname{adj}(A) = \det(A) I_n. \]

Step 2 · Take determinants of both sides: Using the multiplicative property \( \det(M_1 M_2) = \det(M_1) \det(M_2) \): \[ \det(A \operatorname{adj}(A)) = \det(\det(A) I_n). \] \[ \det(A) \cdot \det(\operatorname{adj}(A)) = [\det(A)]^n \det(I_n) = [\det(A)]^n (1) = [\det(A)]^n. \]

Step 3 · Divide by \( \det(A) \): Since \( A \) is invertible, \( \det(A) \neq 0 \). Dividing both sides by \( \det(A) \) yields: \[ \mathbf{\det(\operatorname{adj}(A)) = [\det(A)]^{n-1}}. \quad \blacksquare \]
